analysis.one_liner: Funds state red-flag gun laws and bars people under such court orders from buying firearms.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, markup, or vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee from February 2023 until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give federal grants to states, tribes, and local governments that have "red flag" laws, which let courts temporarily order guns removed from people found to be a danger to themselves or others. It would also make people subject to those court orders prohibited from buying or possessing firearms under federal law, require courts' orders to show up in background-check databases, and require other states to enforce the orders. It never received any committee or floor action.
analysis.who_benefits: People at risk of shooting themselves or others — especially in gun suicide and domestic violence situations — along with their families, who would gain a funded, enforceable court process to temporarily separate an at-risk person from firearms. State, tribal, and local courts and police would get money and training to run the process, including crisis intervention and referrals to mental health and social services. Gun dealers and sellers would be blocked from completing sales to people under qualifying orders.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of gun violence

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Justice Department grant program for states, tribes, and local governments that pass red-flag laws, covering personnel, court protocols, safe firearm removal and storage, and public awareness, with at least 25% of grant money required to go to law-enforcement training

Requires grant recipients to train police in de-escalation, crisis intervention, anti-bias practices, domestic-violence safety planning, and referral of people under orders to mental health, housing, employment, and veterans services

Adds people subject to a qualifying extreme risk protection order — one issued after a hearing with notice and an opportunity to participate, with a finding that the person is a danger — to the federal list of people prohibited from buying or possessing guns and ammunition

Requires orders to be entered into the national background-check system and lets the FBI collect records from federal, tribal, and state courts identifying people under such orders, so a prohibited person cannot pass a background check in another state

Requires other states and tribal courts to give full faith and credit to qualifying orders, so an order follows the person across state lines, and guarantees the person named gets notice and a hearing within 30 days

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the grants, which are authorized at 'such sums as are necessary' with no dollar cap. People placed under a court order would lose access to firearms they own, with guns held for return only after they regain legal eligibility. Gun sellers would forgo sales to people under qualifying orders, and states would have to pass laws meeting the federal minimum standards to become eligible for the money.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; gun owners under orders

drawbacks.text: Courts could issue temporary 'ex parte' orders and have guns removed before the named person has been heard, based on a probable-cause finding by one judge; the person's first chance to respond comes at a later hearing, which the bill says must happen within 30 days

The federal gun ban under this bill applies only to orders issued after a full hearing with notice and participation, but state-law temporary orders could still result in firearms being surrendered first and contested afterward

Grant money is conditional: a state or tribe only qualifies if it enacts legislation meeting detailed federal minimums, and between 25% and 70% of the money must be spent on law-enforcement training rather than services, which critics of federal grants call strings attached to local priorities

The FBI would compile records from federal, tribal, and state courts identifying individuals subject to extreme risk protection orders in national crime-information databases, which raises privacy concerns about lists of people who have not been convicted of any crime
The grant program is authorized at 'such sums as are necessary' — an open-ended appropriation with no cost ceiling for taxpayers

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — a funded court process to temporarily separate people in crisis from firearms, with a federal backup so orders show up in background checks — targets gun suicide and domestic violence, two of the largest categories of gun death. The bill builds in real due-process guardrails: notice, a hearing within 30 days, a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard or higher, a ban on destroying confiscated guns without the owner's consent, and a federal prohibition that only applies to orders issued after a contested hearing. The strongest honest objection is the ex parte step, where a judge can order removal before the person has been heard, and the open-ended, uncapped appropriation. It is a deliberately cautious version of a policy that roughly twenty states had already adopted, and its main cost falls on a narrow group of people a court found dangerous rather than on the public broadly.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Salud Carbajal introduced the bill on February 2, 2023, joined as original cosponsors by Reps. Don Beyer and Julia Brownley
Nine House Democrats cosponsored the bill in total, all from the minority party in the chamber
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction, and the action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote at any point afterward
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with the bill still sitting in committee, so it died without any vote ever being scheduled

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of red-flag laws and the gun industry are better off: no new federal prohibition was created, no orders were added to background-check databases, and no federal money went into state and tribal red-flag programs. People who feared ex parte firearm removal also avoided the policy taking effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents of red-flag laws and the gun industry

for.name: Rep. Salud Carbajal
for.role: Sponsor; member of the House Armed Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited nine cosponsors

against.name: Rep. Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill with no action beyond referral for the full two-year Congress

against.name: Speaker Kevin McCarthy
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so no split is recorded: all 9 cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled House Judiciary Committee took no action after referral.

industries.note: The bill would bar people under qualifying court orders from buying or possessing guns and enter those orders into background checks, cutting off sales to that group. Industry-aligned opposition to red-flag laws is one reason such measures stall in Congress.

industries.industry: State, tribal, and local law enforcement and courts
industries.note: Grant funds would pay for personnel, training, court protocols, and safe firearm storage, with 25-70% of the money earmarked for law-enforcement training. Police would gain a court-backed tool for the highest-risk cases.

industries.industry: Community mental health and domestic-violence service providers
industries.note: Grants would fund training in crisis intervention and referral of people under orders to mental health, substance abuse, housing, and legal services, and recipients must consult domestic-violence service providers when designing training.
